title: Hot-water crust pastry for raised pies
subtitle: The pastry that is moulded warm and holds its shape as it cools
excerpt: Hot-water crust is made by pouring boiling water and melted lard into flour, then kneading while warm. The heat creates a pliable, workable pastry that can be hand-raised into a free-standing pie without a tin. It sets firm as it cools, holding walls straight and thick enough to carry a dense meat filling.
sourceNotes: Hot-water crust pastry is documented in Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, and in Mrs Rundell, A New System of Domestic Cookery (1806). The lard-and-boiling-water method for hand-raised pies is a traditional British technique used for pork pies and game pies.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough for a 450 g raised pie or one 20 cm pie tin
recipe.freezeNotes: Hot-water crust does not freeze well before use; it becomes brittle on thawing. Freeze the finished, baked pie instead.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Use the pastry while still warm and pliable. It sets firm as it cools and cannot be re-worked easily once cold.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven; fan 180°C, start hot to set the crust, then drop to 170°C conventional for the final 30 minutes

content.text: Hot-water crust is the pastry of the classic British pork pie: dense, robust walls raised without a tin, firm enough to slice cold and carry in a box. The pastry is made with boiling water and lard and must be shaped while still warm before it stiffens.

350 g strong white flour (the higher protein helps the structure), 125 g lard, 150 ml water, 1 tsp salt. For a lighter version, replace half the lard with butter, the flavour is richer but the pastry slightly softer.
Sift the flour and salt into a bowl and make a well in the centre.
Bring the lard and water to a rolling boil in a small saucepan. The fat should be fully melted. Pour immediately into the flour.
Beat together with a wooden spoon until the dough comes away from the bowl. It will be very hot, wait a couple of minutes before handling.
Turn onto a floured surface and knead briefly. Reserve one quarter of the dough for the lid. Use the remaining three quarters immediately while still warm and pliable.

Press the warm dough up and around the outside of a jar or straight-sided mould to an even 8 to 10 mm wall thickness. Work quickly before it cools. Once cool it can be removed from the mould and will hold its shape. Trim the top edge level and fill, then apply the lid and crimp the edges together.
Cover the reserved lid pastry with a warm damp cloth while you shape the case. Cold pastry becomes stiff and cracks when pressed.
